title: Charts: bar and line

cells.text: Charts make patterns jump out. Any pandas summary can draw itself with `.plot()`, and the chart appears right under the cell. The usual recipe: **summarise first** (value_counts or groupby), **then** add `.plot()`.

cells.prompt: Press Run to load the games table.
cells.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("games.csv")
df.head()

cells.text: `kind="bar"` draws a bar chart, which is best for comparing categories like genres. One bar is drawn per row of the summary.

cells.prompt: There are 11 different genres. How many bars will this chart have? Pick one, then press Run.
Replace ___ with "bar" (in quotes) to draw the genre counts as a bar chart, then press Run.
hints: The chart kind is text, so it needs quotes.

cells.text: Add `title="..."` inside plot() to label the chart, for example `.plot(kind="bar", title="Games per genre")`.
`kind="line"` draws a line chart, which is best for change over time, like years. The summary must be in time order, and groupby sorts the years for you.

cells.prompt: Press Run to see how many games came out each year, as a line.
Your turn: draw a bar chart of the average rating per genre, highest first. Summarise with groupby, sort, then plot.
hints: groupby genre, pick rating, mean, sort_values(ascending=False), then .plot(kind="bar").

cells.text: You can also plot straight from the table. `df.plot(kind="barh", x="title", y="price")` draws sideways bars (h for horizontal), with x as the labels and y as the bar lengths. Sideways bars are easier to read when the labels are long.

cells.prompt: Last one: draw a sideways bar chart of every game's price, with the titles as the labels.
hints: Copy the example: df.plot(kind="barh", x="title", y="price")

recap: Summarise first, then .plot(). kind="bar" compares categories, kind="line" shows change over time, and kind="barh" gives sideways bars. title="..." labels the chart.
